name: Gboard (Google Keyboard)
evidence_basis: Google official Gboard Help articles, APK teardowns (Android Police / 9to5Google / Android Authority / XDA), and community reverse-engineering tooling (Rboard Theme Manager, Rboard Theme Creator, Magisk theme modules). No official theme SDK or format spec is published by Google; internal-format claims below come from community tooling and are flagged accordingly.
rendering_approach: Hybrid, and this is the single most important thing to copy. Gboard composites in three layers: (1) a whole-image background paste that spans the entire keyboard surface (the user's photo, or a flat/gradient color for built-in themes), (2) a dimming scrim over that image, (3) a per-key layer drawn on top whose keys are transparent by default and only acquire their own visible background/border drawable when the user turns 'Key borders' on. This is why the 'Key borders' toggle exists at all: without it there is no per-key drawable and labels sit directly on the photo; with it, each key gets its own rounded-rect background so the label has a local surface. Key labels/glyphs themselves are drawn as a separate top layer and, for photo themes, are fixed to white and are NOT user-recolorable on Android (multiple guides explicitly state 'the buttons are white and can't be changed'), which is the deliberate simplification that makes the whole system safe. For non-photo built-in and Dynamic Color themes, the model degrades to conventional per-key drawing: solid background color + per-key-role fill colors, no image layer. On iOS (Gboard 2.0+), the per-key layer is far more configurable - letter keys and functional keys are separate targets, each with independently toggleable background and border, plus themeable text. [uncertain - the three-layer decomposition is inferred from consistent user-facing behavior and screenshots across many sources, not from published Google documentation or decompiled render code]
selector_and_state_model: No public rule syntax exists - Gboard has no author-facing selector language, only a fixed set of internal style slots. What is observable as targetable: (a) key ROLE - Gboard distinguishes 'letter keys' from 'non-text keys' / functional keys (backspace, enter, period, shift/caps, ?123, comma/emoji, the menu/overflow button); the Android Dynamic Color rollout was reported specifically as collapsing 'three different colors for the non-letter keys' down to one accent pulled from the Material You palette, which confirms functional keys were historically split into multiple role buckets (action/enter vs modifier vs punctuation). (b) key SURFACE ELEMENT - on iOS each role exposes background, border, and text as separate settable properties. (c) key POPUP as its own target - iOS exposes key-popup background color and text color independently of the key itself. (d) GLIDE TRAIL as its own target - trail color plus trail thickness (slider), plus an on/off 'swipe trail sparkles' decoration. Pressed state is implied by the existence of a distinct pressed/highlight color in themes but is not separately exposed to users. Shift/caps state, disabled state, and per-key-code targeting are not exposed in any user-facing surface and are not documented anywhere public. Google explicitly notes 'not all theme options are applicable for some Chinese and Japanese keyboard layouts', implying the style slots are keyed to a Latin-layout role taxonomy that some IME layouts do not fully populate. [uncertain - role taxonomy is reconstructed from feature journalism and the settings UI, not from a published schema; there is no confirmed selector/rule syntax]
rendering_pipeline: Android: classic View/Canvas/Drawable inside an InputMethodService, not Jetpack Compose. Gboard descends from AOSP LatinIME, which drew keys via a custom View with Canvas + 9-patch Drawables and StateListDrawables, and Gboard's per-keystroke behavior (immediate invalidate of a small key rect rather than full-tree recomposition) is consistent with that lineage. Compose is a known poor fit inside an InputMethodService because the service is not a LifecycleOwner/ViewModelStoreOwner/SavedStateRegistryOwner by default and must be shimmed, which is likely part of why Google has not migrated. iOS: UIKit-based custom views inside a keyboard app extension, not SwiftUI. Per-keystroke cost is kept low by invalidating only the touched key's bounds; the background image is decoded once at theme-apply time rather than per frame. [uncertain - the AOSP-lineage and no-Compose claims are strong inference from Gboard's history and from Android platform constraints, not from decompiled Gboard code; Google publishes nothing here]
compositing_scrim_model: Stack order, bottom to top: background image (or flat/gradient color) -> brightness/dim scrim -> optional per-key background+border layer -> key labels/glyphs -> key-press popup and glide trail. The scrim is the load-bearing legibility mechanism and is exposed to the user as a single 'brightness' slider, described in multiple sources as literally 'adjusting the percentage of black overlay' - i.e. a black rectangle at variable alpha over the photo, not a per-pixel luminance operation. Lower slider value = darker composite. Community guidance is consistent and worth noting as a design constant: users are told to keep brightness BELOW ~40% because key labels are fixed white, so anything brighter loses the labels. Gboard does not expose a blur, and does not expose scrim color (black only). There is no published default value for the slider on Android - Gboard opens the brightness step as an explicit required step in the flow after cropping, so the user always makes a choice rather than accepting a documented default. This contrasts with SwiftKey, which documents a 45% default. Gradient built-in themes are a separate background type (flat two-stop gradient) rather than an image, and take no scrim. [uncertain - 'black overlay at variable alpha' is how third-party guides describe it and matches the visual result, but Google's own help text only says 'brightness'; the exact blend mode and whether it is black-over vs. a multiply/alpha-luminance filter is not documented]
asset_types: For user-created photo themes the asset is a single plain raster image taken from the device gallery (JPEG/PNG/HEIF as delivered by the system photo picker), re-encoded and stored per-theme after crop. For built-in themes and for the per-key layer, assets are Android resource drawables - the AOSP LatinIME lineage used 9-patch PNGs for key backgrounds (stretchable rounded-rect key caps across variable key widths) plus vector drawables for functional-key glyphs; modern Gboard has moved most key-cap rendering toward vector/shape drawables and programmatic rounded rects, consistent with the Material 3 rounded-corner refresh. Community theme packs distributed through Rboard are described as 'a collection of image assets, style sheets, and metadata', i.e. rasters plus a declarative style layer. Density bucketing (mdpi/hdpi/xhdpi/xxhdpi) applies to the bundled drawable resources as with any Android app, but does NOT apply to user photo themes, which are a single image scaled at runtime. [uncertain - the 9-patch vs. programmatic-shape split in current Gboard is inferred from lineage and visual evidence, not verified against decompiled resources]
theme_package_manifest_format: There is no public, documented, supported theme package format - Google ships no theme SDK and no third-party theme store for Gboard. Everything known comes from the root-only community ecosystem. Community consensus, primarily from Rboard Theme Manager / Rboard Theme Creator and the XDA scene: a Gboard theme pack carries a '.pack' extension and is 'essentially a collection of image assets, style sheets, and metadata - all compressed under a special container format' (proprietary container, not a plain zip; Rboard also distributes 'stable' variants as .zip). Gboard is known to have migrated its internal config/flag storage from XML to protocol buffers, so the style-sheet and metadata members inside a pack are widely believed to be binary protobuf ('.binarypb'-style) rather than JSON or XML - this is consistent with Gboard's flag system but is NOT confirmed for theme packs specifically. Install locations differ by delivery route: Magisk/system modules place theme files under /system/etc/gboard_themes/ and set two system properties to point Gboard at that directory; Rboard Theme Manager instead writes into Gboard's own private app data directory, which is why it requires root. No manifest filename, no field list, and no folder layout have ever been published. A theming implementation should treat Gboard as a reference for UX and layering, NOT as a format to copy - the format is undocumented, proprietary, root-gated, and both major community managers (RboardThemeManagerV3, Gboardthemer) are now archived/discontinued. [uncertain - .pack container internals, protobuf encoding, and manifest field names are all unverified community inference; the /system/etc/gboard_themes path and the two-system-property mechanism are the only concretely documented facts]
token_count_tiering: No official token count exists. Two clearly distinct tiers are observable in the shipping product: SIMPLE tier (the only one most users see) = pick a built-in theme, or pick a photo + crop + brightness + key-borders on/off - roughly 3-4 user-settable properties on Android. ADVANCED tier appears on iOS via Gboard 2.0, which exposes ~4 customizable AREAS (Background, Keys, Key popups, Glide typing) with roughly 8-12 settable properties across them: background color (28 built-in variants including gradients), letter-key background on/off, letter-key border on/off, letter-key text color, functional-key background on/off, functional-key border on/off, functional-key text color, key-popup background color, key-popup text color, glide trail color, glide trail thickness, glide sparkles on/off. The internal style sheet almost certainly carries far more slots than any UI exposes - Rboard Patcher users report editing 'different aspects of the themes' well beyond the official settings, and an APK teardown as far back as Gboard v6.8 flagged a 'new theme engine' and later a 'third version of the theme feature' giving 'more control over the look'. A defensible planning number: expose a simple tier of ~4 controls and an advanced tier of ~12-15 tokens; that brackets what Gboard actually ships. [uncertain - the ~12 iOS property count is enumerated from feature coverage of Gboard 2.0 and may have drifted; the internal slot count is unknown]
theme_versioning_forward_compat: Not publicly documented. The community ecosystem gives indirect evidence that versioning is weak and brittle: Rboard theme packs are distributed in per-Gboard-version 'stable' vs 'beta' streams, community themes routinely break on Gboard updates, and both major manager apps were ultimately archived. That pattern is what you get when the format is an internal serialization with no stability contract rather than a versioned public schema. Since themes are internal-only from Google's side, Google can and does change slots freely between releases. Treat as: no schema version guarantee, unknown unknown-property handling. [uncertain - entirely inferred from ecosystem breakage patterns; no version field has ever been documented]
color_extraction_dynamic_tinting: Both models coexist, cleanly separated. PRE-BAKED: built-in themes and user photo themes carry fixed color values (photo themes in particular hard-fix key labels to white rather than deriving them from the image). DYNAMIC: Gboard shipped a 'Dynamic Color' theme built on Android 12's Material You / 'monet' engine - it consumes the system palette that Android derives from the user's wallpaper, rather than running its own Palette-API extraction on the keyboard background. Requires Android 12+; prepped in Gboard 10.7 (June 2021) and rolled out through 2021. Behavior: the lightest hue of the Material You palette becomes the keyboard background in light mode, most keys stay white when key borders are on, and functional keys take other palette roles. Google later tested collapsing the three separate functional-key colors down to a single dynamic accent applied to shift, ?123, comma/emoji, period, enter, backspace and the menu button. Notably, Gboard does NOT extract colors from a user's own photo theme to tint labels or keys - the photo path deliberately avoids extraction and relies on the fixed-white-label + scrim strategy instead. That is a meaningful design signal: extraction is used only where the source palette is already system-vetted. Gboard on iOS has no equivalent dynamic-color path.
contrast_enforcement_accessibility: There is no evidence of any automated WCAG/APCA contrast validation of composited output. Gboard instead uses three structural guarantees that make validation unnecessary for the photo path: (1) key labels are FIXED WHITE and not user-editable on Android photo themes - removing the entire class of 'user picked a light label on a light photo' failures; (2) the brightness scrim is a mandatory step in the creation flow, so the user is always forced to darken the photo before committing; (3) the 'Key borders' toggle is the explicit escape hatch - turning it on gives every key its own opaque/semi-opaque background so labels sit on a controlled local surface rather than on arbitrary photo pixels. Community guidance (keep brightness under ~40%, avoid busy photos in the key region) does the rest, which is an admission that the burden is on the user, not the system. Separately, Android's system-level high-contrast text and OEM accessibility settings can affect rendering, and the 'Key borders' setting doubles as an accessibility feature - sources describe it as 'separating one key from another, making it easier to tap a character and reducing wrong key presses'. Net: legibility is engineered-by-constraint (fixed labels + forced scrim + border escape hatch), not measured. This is the single most transferable lesson from Gboard. [uncertain - the absence of automated contrast checking is an inference from the absence of any such claim or observable behavior; Google has never stated either way]
background_geometry_adaptation: Gboard's answer is: fit the image to the keyboard rect at theme-creation time via an explicit user crop, then scale that fixed crop to whatever the keyboard rect later becomes. The creation flow presents a crop/position step described as 'Pinch to Scale, Drag to Move' against a boundary box shaped like the keyboard, so the user - not an algorithm - resolves the aspect-ratio decision once. Afterward the keyboard rect varies a lot and Gboard must stretch/scale the same crop: height is user-resizable (Gboard's resize can take the keyboard from roughly a third of the screen up to three-quarters, and newer builds add free drag-resize), one-handed mode shrinks it to about half width with a settable side, split mode divides it down the middle in landscape and on tablets/foldables, and since late 2023 Gboard automatically switches to a FLOATING keyboard on rotation to landscape - a movable, resizable, repositionable window that remembers its last position across apps and rotations. The floating case is the hardest: the background must render inside a small free-floating rounded window rather than a full-width strip. Gboard's practical mitigation is that its own photo backgrounds are treated as decorative rather than layout-registered - nothing in the image needs to land on a specific key - so scaling artifacts degrade gracefully. There is no published documentation of the exact scale mode (center-crop vs. fit-xy) per configuration. Design implication for a clone: never let theme art be positionally load-bearing, and always re-scale the single stored crop rather than storing per-configuration variants. [uncertain - the specific scaling/crop mode applied in floating, split, and one-handed configurations is not documented and community reports do not cover it precisely]
layout_locale_independence: Gboard's photo-theme model is layout-independent by construction: the background is a single image behind the whole keyboard with no per-key registration, so turning the number row on or off, switching to AZERTY/QWERTZ/Dvorak, switching to a non-Latin script layout, or flipping to an RTL locale changes only the key grid drawn on top - the art does not need to know. The per-key layer is generated from the live layout, so key count and key widths are free variables. The known limit is on the ADVANCED per-role tier, not the background tier: Google explicitly documents that 'not all theme options are applicable for some Chinese and Japanese keyboard layouts', which is exactly the failure mode you would expect when a style system keys its slots to a Latin key-role taxonomy (shift / ?123 / period / comma-emoji) that CJK IME layouts populate differently or not at all. Split layouts are handled by the geometry adaptation path rather than by anything layout-semantic. Takeaway: whole-image background = fully layout/locale independent; per-role token maps = partially layout-bound and need a documented fallback for roles a given layout does not have.
non_key_surface_coverage: Coverage is broad and extends beyond the keyboard's own bounds - notably including a system surface. Confirmed covered: the suggestion/prediction strip and the toolbar row above the keys (they sit on the same background surface); the emoji / GIF / sticker panel, which follows the theme and was itself restyled with rounded-rect containers for the emoji/sticker/GIF icons in the 2025 Material 3 refresh; key-press popups, which on iOS are a first-class independently themeable target (background + text color); and the ANDROID SYSTEM NAVIGATION BAR - since a 2019 update, and expanded to more devices in August 2022, Gboard tints the nav bar to match the active keyboard theme instead of the previous black-or-white-only behavior, which visually merges the keyboard with the bottom of the screen. This is a strong UX detail worth copying and is achievable from an IME via window/nav-bar color APIs. Less certain: the long-press mini-keyboard (accent picker), the clipboard manager sheet, and the in-keyboard settings sheets appear to follow the theme's surface colors but are not separately documented or separately settable. Gboard's own settings screens inside the host app are themed by the app's Material design (Material 3 Expressive refresh in progress), independent of the keyboard theme. [uncertain - long-press mini-keyboard, clipboard sheet, and in-keyboard settings coverage is observational rather than documented]
sound_haptic_theming: Not themed. Sound and haptics are global keyboard PREFERENCES, fully decoupled from the visual theme: Gboard's Preferences > 'Key press' section exposes 'Sound on keypress', 'Volume on keypress', 'Haptic feedback on keypress', and 'Vibration strength on keypress'. There is no per-theme sound pack, no swappable click sample, and no way for a theme to carry audio. Implementation is the standard Android path - AudioManager/SoundPool for the click and HapticFeedbackConstants/Vibrator for the tick - and Google documents the important gotcha that device-level vibration settings override Gboard's own. Note this is a deliberate divergence from Samsung, whose Keys Cafe DOES bundle sound and animation into a keyboard style. [uncertain - the specific Android audio/haptic APIs used internally are inferred from platform norms, not documented]
platform_apis_frameworks: Android: InputMethodService + a custom key View hierarchy drawn with Canvas and Drawable/StateListDrawable/9-patch (AOSP LatinIME lineage), the Android resource system with density buckets, the system photo picker for background selection, Android 12+ Material You / 'monet' dynamic color APIs for the Dynamic Color theme, and window/navigation-bar color APIs for nav-bar tinting. Protocol buffers are used for Gboard's internal config/flag storage (migrated away from XML). Theme feature rollout is server-driven via Google's own feature-flag infrastructure, which is why theme features appear staged and A/B-tested. iOS: a keyboard app extension (UIInputViewController) with UIKit custom views, plus the containing Gboard app for theme creation UI; Full Access is required for the app and extension to share state. [uncertain - specific internal class/framework choices are inferred; Google publishes no architecture documentation for Gboard]
delivery_installation_pipeline: There is no supported third-party theme delivery pipeline for Gboard - this is the defining fact. Three real routes exist: (1) BUNDLED - all built-in themes ship inside the Gboard APK/IPA as app resources and are gated/rolled out by server-side feature flags; users cannot add to this set. (2) USER-GENERATED, LOCAL ONLY - photo themes are created in-app from a gallery image, cropped, dimmed, and stored in Gboard's own private app data on that device. They are not signed, not shareable, not exportable, and do not travel between devices; Android users can create unlimited custom background themes and delete them individually. (3) COMMUNITY, ROOT-ONLY - third-party '.pack' themes reach Gboard either via a Magisk/system module that drops files into /system/etc/gboard_themes/ and rewrites two system properties to point Gboard at that directory, or via Rboard Theme Manager writing directly into Gboard's private data directory. Both require root; Rboard's docs are explicit that 'the app needs root access to run'. Contrast with SwiftKey (official downloadable theme gallery) and Samsung (signed theme APKs through Galaxy Themes / Theme Center): Google deliberately did not build a theme distribution channel, and both major community managers are now archived. If you are designing a theme marketplace, Gboard is the wrong model to copy for DELIVERY and the right model to copy for the single-photo CREATION flow.
permission_store_policy_surface: Android: no special permission is needed for the photo path because Gboard uses the system photo picker, which grants access to only the chosen image without requiring READ_MEDIA_IMAGES/READ_EXTERNAL_STORAGE. Binding an IME requires the user to explicitly enable and switch keyboards through system settings, and Android surfaces the standard 'this input method may collect all text you type' warning. Because Gboard has no third-party theme content, Google Play's policies around user-generated and downloadable content simply do not apply to it - there is no moderation surface, no theme review, and no dynamic-content review risk. That absence is itself the policy strategy. iOS: the Gboard keyboard extension requires Full Access (RequestsOpenAccess) for the app and extension to share data, which is what lets a theme created in the containing app apply inside the extension; Apple shows a privacy warning when the user grants it. Any product that DOES ship downloadable themes inherits obligations Gboard avoided: App Store review of dynamically delivered content, executable-code restrictions (theme content must be pure data/assets, never code), and Play's UGC moderation and reporting requirements. [uncertain - the specific claim that Gboard uses the modern photo picker rather than a storage permission is inferred from current Android norms and Gboard's lack of a storage permission prompt]
memory_performance_budget: Android has no hard per-IME memory ceiling, and Gboard is empirically heavy - user reports cite roughly 250 MB RSS, and Google shipped a separate cut-down 'Gboard Go' variant using about half the RAM (dropping GIF search, stickers, and one-handed mode) for Android Go / low-memory devices. That is the real budget signal: Google's answer to memory pressure was a whole second SKU, not a smaller theme system. iOS is the binding constraint and is where the discipline shows: Apple's keyboard extension limit is roughly 30-40 MB dirty memory (about 77 MB total footprint) before the extension is killed, and a decoded full-resolution photo alone can blow that - a 12 MP image at 4 bytes/px is ~48 MB decoded, i.e. instant death. Gboard's structural mitigations, visible in behavior: the photo is cropped and re-encoded ONCE at theme-creation time in the containing app (which has a normal app memory budget) rather than in the extension; the extension loads only the pre-processed, keyboard-sized bitmap; and Gboard permits no animated backgrounds at all, so there is no video/GIF decoder resident in the extension. Concrete guidance this implies for a clone: downsample to the maximum keyboard rect across supported configurations (roughly device-width x ~40% of screen height at native scale), decode with an explicit sample size, cache exactly one decoded background bitmap and evict on theme switch, and do the crop/encode work in the host app, never in the extension. [uncertain - the '~250 MB' figure comes from user forum reports across unspecified versions; the crop-in-host-app division of labor is inferred from the UI flow, not documented]
untrusted_theme_validation_security: Effectively out of scope for Gboard as shipped, because Gboard never ingests untrusted theme content - built-in themes are compiled in, and user photo themes come from the device's own photo picker. There is no zip extraction path, so no zip-slip surface; there is no third-party manifest, so no malformed-manifest handling. The only untrusted input is the user's own image, decoded through the platform image decoders (BitmapFactory / ImageDecoder / ImageIO), which carry the platform's own hardening. The community '.pack' route bypasses all of this by requiring root and writing directly into Gboard's private data - an explicitly unsafe trust model that only works because the user has already granted root. Note the asymmetry: an app that DOES accept downloaded theme zips must add path-traversal checks on every zip entry, decode-bounds limits, entry-count/uncompressed-size limits (zip bomb), and strict manifest schema validation - none of which Gboard needed. [uncertain - no security documentation exists for Gboard theming; this is a structural analysis of the attack surface rather than a report of implemented mitigations]
open_source_reference_availability: Gboard itself is fully closed source - no theming module is published, and Google ships no theme SDK, format spec, or authoring documentation. Two useful proxies exist. (1) LINEAGE: AOSP LatinIME (packages/inputmethods/LatinIME in the Android source tree) is Gboard's open-source ancestor and its KeyboardTheme / key-background StateListDrawable / 9-patch key-cap approach is directly readable and is the best available model for how per-key drawing worked before Gboard forked. (2) COMMUNITY TOOLING, now mostly archived: github.com/DerTyp7214/RboardThemeManagerV3 (archived April 2026), github.com/nitanmarcel/GboardThemePacks, github.com/catppuccin/rboard (theme collection), github.com/nylonW/gboard_themes (Magisk module, documents the /system/etc/gboard_themes path), github.com/iamimmanuelraj/Gboardthemer (archived March 2026). These show WHAT the format roughly contains but not its schema. Practical conclusion: study Gboard for UX, study LatinIME for rendering, and take your actual format from an open-source keyboard (FlorisBoard, OpenBoard, HeliBoard) or from SwiftKey's better-documented community format.
authoring_tooling_preview_generation: First-party: no external theme editor and no theme SDK - authoring is entirely in-app and consumer-grade. The in-app flow is crop (pinch-to-scale / drag-to-move against a keyboard-shaped boundary box) -> brightness slider -> key-borders toggle -> Done, with a LIVE PREVIEW KEYBOARD rendered in real time at each step so the user judges legibility against actual key labels before committing; on iOS every theme tile carries a pencil edit affordance that opens the same real-time preview, and finished custom themes appear in a carousel at the top of the themes page. Because there is no theme store, there are no store-thumbnail or multi-variant preview requirements at all - the 'thumbnail' is just the theme tile rendered from the theme itself. Third-party (root scene, historical): Rboard Theme Creator is an on-device Android app that compiles a themepack without a PC, driven by a rotating color dial with scheme selection (Dark, Monet) and component selection (AMOLED, Tertiary Accent), with a live preview section and export via a share sheet capturing name + author metadata; the same developer hosted a web version for desktop authoring, and Rboard Patcher allowed deeper post-hoc editing. Transferable lesson: live preview on the real key grid during authoring is what substitutes for automated contrast checking.
cross_platform_token_parity: No parity, and no shared theme definition. Android and iOS Gboard are separate implementations with divergent - in places inverted - feature sets, and no theme artifact crosses between them. Android-only: unlimited user-created photo themes with an explicit crop + brightness + key-borders flow, Material You Dynamic Color (Android 12+ only, since it depends on the OS palette), and navigation-bar tinting (no iOS equivalent - iOS has no such system surface for an extension to tint). iOS-only: the far richer Gboard 2.0 per-element model - 28 color variants including gradients, separate letter-key vs functional-key background/border/text control, independently themeable key popups, and glide-trail color + thickness + sparkles. Photo backgrounds exist on both (added to iOS alongside dark theme in 2019), but the surrounding token sets do not correspond. Inherently platform-bound properties: dynamic/wallpaper color (Android OS palette), nav-bar color (Android only), and anything depending on iOS Full Access for app-to-extension sharing. Design implication: a shared token schema should carry the geometry-independent core (background image reference, crop rect, scrim alpha, key-border on/off, label color) and treat dynamic-color and system-chrome tokens as optional, platform-gated extensions.
animation_budget: OPEN / WEAKLY DOCUMENTED - flag this as a real gap. Gboard supports NO animated theme backgrounds on either platform: no Lottie, no GIF, no video backgrounds, and no live wallpapers behind the keys. Backgrounds are strictly static rasters or flat/gradient colors. The only motion in the theming system is interaction feedback rather than ambient animation: key-press popups, and on iOS the glide-typing trail (settable color and thickness) plus the optional 'swipe trail sparkles' decoration of small multi-colored G logos. Because there is no ambient animation, there is no published frame-rate cap and no idle-pause policy - the questions do not arise. This is almost certainly a deliberate choice driven by the iOS extension memory ceiling and by battery/jank concerns in a surface that must respond to every keystroke within a frame; note that Samsung's Keys Cafe DOES ship key-press animations, so the constraint is a product decision rather than a platform impossibility. No source states Google's reasoning explicitly. [uncertain - the rationale is inferred; the factual claim that no animated backgrounds are supported is well-supported by the complete absence of any such feature in documentation and coverage]
